docs.title: Welcome to the CherryHub
docs.text: I'm a mathematics student at the University of Leipzig and personal tutor. This is a website for showcasing computational projects and a place where I blog about mathematics for anyone interested in my work.

docs.title: Coding projects
docs.text:
I work on various projects involving programming. Mostly, I write in Python, but I also frequently write solutions in Julia. When new stuff is made, you can see it showcased here.

  • The CherryBot Discord App - Multi-purpose bot tool for Discord
  • Orbital - Julia Simulation of Planetary Orbits

docs.title: Math articles
docs.text:
I use this site to post blogs about mathematics. Coming soon, you might also find film theory here. Check out my article on the Calculus of Variations:

The Elegance of Variational Calculus, 5 min read

docs.title: Teaching resources
docs.text:
This is still a work in progress! I'm planning to upload some study sheets and tutoring materials here. Stay up to date if you care about this.

Expect articles on math expressed via Julia scripting or theory behind chess and speedcubing.

docs.title: Who I am
docs.text:
My name is Cherry and I am a German mathematician and teacher. I specialize in developing solutions for computational problems and communicating higher academic mathematics. This website is my personal portfolio for projects I have made as well as a place to publish articles about interesting pieces of math. Feel free to read my work or just see the abstracts to know what it's about. If there's anything you'd like to talk about, feel free to hit me up. I'm always available to chat about my work or take suggestions / error reports.

In my free time, I enjoy reading poetry, solving Rubik's cubes, cycling, playing chess, analyzing films and making art.

This blog was originally started in September 2026. I cannot guarantee regular updates or publications. It's honestly just a for fun project.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Here are some basic steps on how to first get started with the bot. If anything ever doesn't work, you should probably check if you have everything done here. I generally recommend you to check the documentation if anything ever breaks. If this doesn't fix it, the root is something that most definitely but perchance occasionally possibly may have been my fault. Oops.

Before anything else, the most important command:

  • type %report [text] to have a message sent to me directly Whether you have a problem, want to suggest something, whatever. The text will be given to me via bot logs and I will read it ASAP.

docs.title: Setting up an admin role
docs.text:
• this can only be done by the server owner
  • there can only be one role capable of cherrybot-privileges
  • please make sure only trusted members have this role
  • type %admin_add @[some_role]
  • type %adminrole to see the current admin role

docs.title: Setting up a welcome channel
docs.text:
• this assigns a specific channel from your server where a welcome message will be sent
  • this can only be done by someone with the local cherrybot admin role
  • use %welcome_add [mention-channel] to set a new channel or replacing the old one
  • use %welcome_remove to remove the local channel assignment
  • use %welcome_see to see your local channel assignment)

docs.title: Using the to-do feature
docs.text:
There is a server-stored to-do list connected to each cherrybot user. The list is created upon first using a to-do related command.

  • use %todo see to view your to-do list content
  • use %todo add [task] to add [task] to your to-do list
  • use %todo remove [index] to remove the [index]-th task from your to-do list
  • use %todo to quick view an explanation for the three commands

docs.title: [WIP] The Elegance of Variational Calculus
docs.text: What's the fastest path between two points? How do physicists know how light travels? A practical introduction to optimizing functionals.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: If you'd like to read this text, you should be fluent in single variable calculus. Without knowing what a derivative or integral is, you probably won't get far here. The main results are in form of differential equations. Don't feel intimidated if you haven't had much contact with those.

docs.title: The Brachistochrone Problem
docs.text:
Problem setup

As you can see, using some basic physics and calculus, we can rearrange the problem of finding the optimal curve to optimizing the following function for a \(y\) that gives the smallest \(T[y]\). \(T[y]=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}dx\) For now, this might seem like just another complicated way to write the same problem. But bear with me, this will be our way to success later on. However, before being able to explore this problem better, we should take a brief sidetrack into the theory of so-called "Variational Calculus".

docs.title: Basics in Variational Calculus
docs.text: The following section of this article will focus on proving the main result in Variational Calculus. Developing the "Euler-Lagrange Equation" will be the climax of this topic for most purposes. The result is highly elegant, in fact deserving of the title as my personal favorite equation, but note that the derivation of it will be quite intense. Make sure to take your time following the steps or possibly skim it if you don't feel well-versed in calculus.

docs.title: Deriving the Euler-Lagrange Equation
docs.text:
In the following, we will try to establish a necessary condition for a function \(f\) to be extremal considering a functional. Remember that the condition is not sufficient, yet going from the entire function space to the solutions of a differential equation is highly useful for our studies. In the following, consider this shape of functional:

\[J[y]:=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} L(x,y(x),y'(x))dx\]

Here, \(L(x,y(x),y'(x))\) shall be a given function that is at least twice continuously differentiable. The function \(y\) is our independent variable. It shall be twice continuously differentiable and satisfy the boundary conditions \(y(x_1)=y_1, y(x_2)=y_2\). Now, we use a perturbation on our functional. That perturbation is a twice continuously differentiable function commonly denoted \(\eta(x)\). The considered point/function where \(J[y]\) reaches a local minimum/maximum shall be called \(f\). We are now dealing with a new function \(H(\epsilon):=J[y+\epsilon\eta]\). Notice that to keep the edge conditions we need to set \(\eta(x_1)=\eta(x_2)=0\). This now means that our new function \(H(\epsilon)\) has a minimum at \(\epsilon = 0\). This goes analogously to the standard method in single variable calculus. We can now say that

\[H'(0)=\frac{dH}{d\epsilon}\Big|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{dL}{d\epsilon}\Big|_{\epsilon=0}dx=0.\]

Consider \(y=f+\epsilon\cdot\eta\) as a function of \(\epsilon\). The term inside the integral can be replaced using the derivative of \(L\) with respect to \(\epsilon\).

\[\frac{dL}{d\epsilon}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{d\epsilon}+\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}\frac{dy'}{d\epsilon}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\eta+\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}\eta'\]

Notice that the last step follows directly from our definition for \(\eta\) since \(y=f+\epsilon\eta, y'=f'+\epsilon\eta'\) which means that \(\frac{dy}{d\epsilon}=\eta\) and \(\frac{dy'}{d\epsilon}=\eta'\).

This result is highly valuable to us, as we can now rewrite our expression for the integral above.

\[\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{dL}{d\epsilon}\Big|_{\epsilon=0}dx=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial f}\eta+\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'}\eta' \right)dx\]

Notice that \(y\) becomes \(f\) as we applied the condition \(\epsilon=0\). Performing an integration by parts on this expression:

\[0=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial f}\eta+\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'}\eta' \right)dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\partial L}{\partial f}\eta \; dx+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial f'}\eta\Big|_{x_1}^{x_2}-\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\eta\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'} \; dx\] \[=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial f}\eta - \eta\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'} \right)dx\]

It becomes clear that the boundary term must vanish since we earlier defined that \(\eta\) evaluated at both \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) has to be \(0\).

We now have the result that for every perturbation \(\eta\) of the function \(f\):

\[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial f} - \frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'} \right)\eta \; dx =0\]

This can be finished off using the "Fundamental Lemma of Variational Calculus".
